title: Duties 3–4: communication & leadership
blurb: Communicating well, protecting confidentiality, keeping good records, and showing leadership in the team even as a newly qualified nurse.
question: The assessor says: "Give me an example of how you've overcome a barrier to communication, and an example of when you've shown leadership." You're a trainee, not a manager. What examples could you use, and how do you show they meet duties 3 and 4?

teach.body: Duty 3 is to "communicate effectively, maintaining confidentiality and records appropriately". Duty 4 is to "provide professional leadership within the team working in partnership with patients, dental teams, other health and social care professionals". Both are backed by the GDC Standards: communicate effectively with patients (principle 2), maintain and protect patients' information (principle 4), and work with colleagues in a way that is in patients' best interests (principle 6).

Much of what patients tell you isn't spoken. White knuckles on the armrest, a tense jaw or avoiding eye contact can signal anxiety long before a patient says so. Your own body language matters too: sitting at the patient's eye level, a calm tone, and giving them time to answer. Active listening means checking you have understood, for example by summarising what they said. Agreeing a stop signal, such as a raised hand, gives a nervous patient some control.

teach.h: Common barriers and what you can do
head: Barrier
What helps
rows: Professional interpreter, not a child or relative
Face them, speak clearly, write it down
Calm tone, explain each step, stop signal
Plain words, easy-read leaflets, involve carer
Pause, turn off equipment, check understanding
teach.caption: Choosing the right method for the person, whether spoken, written or electronic, is part of duty 3.

teach.body: Patient information is shared only with people who need it to provide care, or where the patient consents or the law requires. Never confirm to a caller that someone is a patient without permission. Records must be contemporaneous (made at the time), complete, accurate and attributable to the person who wrote them, in line with UK GDPR and the Data Protection Act 2018. Dental records are kept for 11 years. Mistakes are corrected openly, never hidden.

Leadership isn't a job title. It means taking professional responsibility, setting a good example and influencing others to give safer, better care. Where appropriate, that includes taking responsibility for the actions of colleagues you supervise, such as a trainee in the decontamination room: showing them how, checking their work and giving helpful feedback. You only delegate a task to someone who is trained, competent and indemnified to do it.

teach.caption: A good practice needs both. You can lead without managing anyone.

steps.sub: Has it worked? Adjust if not

teach.text: "I'm just a trainee, so I don't lead" undersells you. Leadership in duty 4 includes speaking up, role-modelling good practice, supporting a newer colleague and working in partnership with patients and other professionals. Equally, don't claim to manage things you don't.

items: Duty 3: communicate effectively, keep information confidential and records accurate.
Read non-verbal cues, remove barriers, and use professional interpreters.
Records: contemporaneous, complete, accurate, attributable; kept 11 years; errors corrected openly.
Duty 4: leadership is influence and responsibility, not a job title.
Delegate only to colleagues who are trained, competent and indemnified, and support those you supervise.

summary: You can now describe how you communicate with all patients and overcome barriers, protect confidentiality, keep records that meet legal and professional standards, tell management from leadership, and give realistic examples of leadership from your own work as a dental nurse.

A.q: A patient who lip-reads arrives for treatment. What is the best way to communicate with her?
options: Speak more loudly and slowly from behind your mask
Talk to her companion instead of to her
Face her, speak clearly and offer it in writing
Use hand gestures and avoid speaking at all
A.why: Facing a lip-reader so she can see your mouth, speaking clearly at a normal pace and offering written information removes the barrier.

whyNot.0: Shouting distorts lip shapes, and a mask hides them completely.
whyNot.1: Talking past the patient ignores her and damages trust.
whyNot.3: Gestures alone are unreliable; she relies on seeing speech.

A.q: A caller says she is a patient's daughter and asks what time her mother's appointment is. What should you do?
options: Give the time, as she is a close family member
Confirm the day, but not the time, to be safe
Ask for her mother's date of birth, then tell her the time
Not confirm anything without the patient's consent
A.why: Even confirming that someone is a patient is a breach of confidentiality unless the patient has consented. Offer to pass on a message instead.

whyNot.0: Being family does not give a right to a patient's information.
whyNot.1: Confirming the day still discloses confidential information.
whyNot.2: Knowing a date of birth does not prove the patient has consented.

A.q: Which is the best example of leadership, rather than management, by a dental nurse?
options: Proposing and modelling a safer way to pass sharps
Completing the weekly stock order accurately and on time
Filling in the staff holiday rota
Updating the practice's opening hours online
A.why: Leadership is about influencing people and practice for the better, such as proposing and role-modelling a safer routine.

whyNot.1: Stock ordering is a management task: running a system.
whyNot.2: Rotas are a management task: organising people's time.
whyNot.3: Updating opening hours is an administrative task.

B.q: You notice you recorded the wrong tooth in yesterday's notes. How should you correct it?
options: Delete the entry and rewrite it correctly
Add a dated, attributed amendment, keeping the original
Ask the dentist to correct it quietly without mentioning you
Leave it, as the treatment itself was correct
B.why: Errors are corrected openly with a dated amendment, attributed to you, so the original remains visible. Records must never be altered to hide a mistake.

whyNot.0: Deleting an entry hides what was originally written and undermines the record.
whyNot.2: Hiding your part isn't honest, and you are responsible for your own records.
whyNot.3: An inaccurate record could lead to future treatment on the wrong tooth.

B.q: During treatment a patient grips the armrests and her knuckles turn white. What does this most likely show, and what do you do?
options: She is cold; offer her a blanket once treatment is finished
She is comfortable; carry on as planned
She is anxious; let the dentist know and reassure her
She is fainting; lie her flat at once
B.why: Gripping and white knuckles are classic non-verbal signs of anxiety. Let the dentist know so they can pause, and reassure her calmly.

whyNot.0: Gripping the armrests isn't a typical sign of feeling cold.
whyNot.1: This body language suggests distress, not comfort.
whyNot.3: Gripping on its own doesn't suggest fainting; look for pallor, dizziness or loss of consciousness.

B.q: You are supervising a trainee in the decontamination room who wants to skip the inspection step. What should you do?
options: Let it go this once, as the clinic is running late
Report the trainee to the GDC straight away
Finish the job yourself and say nothing
Explain why it matters and check they do it
B.why: Taking responsibility for colleagues you supervise means explaining why inspection matters, making sure it is done and giving feedback.

whyNot.0: Skipping inspection puts patients at risk, however busy the clinic is.
whyNot.1: This is a training issue to handle locally, not a fitness-to-practise matter.
whyNot.2: Doing it yourself without explaining means the trainee doesn't learn.

C.q: A patient who speaks little English brings her 12-year-old son to interpret a consent discussion. What is best practice?
options: Arrange a professional interpreter for the discussion
Let the son interpret, as he knows his mother best
Use a free translation app on your own phone
Proceed using gestures and a written leaflet in English
C.why: A professional interpreter makes sure information is accurate and confidential, and avoids putting a child in an inappropriate role.

whyNot.1: Children shouldn't interpret clinical or consent discussions; accuracy and confidentiality may suffer.
whyNot.2: Personal devices and unverified apps risk errors and data breaches.
whyNot.3: Gestures and an English leaflet won't give her the information needed for valid consent.

C.q: What does "contemporaneous" mean when applied to patient records?
options: Written in modern, plain English with no jargon
Made at the time, or as soon as possible after
Stored digitally on the practice system, not on paper
Reviewed by the dentist every year
C.why: Contemporaneous records are made at the time of care or as soon as possible afterwards, so they are accurate.

whyNot.0: Clear language helps, but that isn't what contemporaneous means.
whyNot.2: Records can be paper or digital; timing is what matters here.
whyNot.3: Annual review isn't what the term means.

C.q: Your manager asks you to have a new receptionist, with no infection control training, clean the surgery between patients. What is the right response?
options: Agree, as cleaning surfaces is a simple task
Agree, as long as the receptionist wears gloves
Only delegate once they are trained and competent
Refuse to discuss it and report the manager to the GDC
C.why: You can only delegate to someone trained and competent for the task. Explain this and suggest training first, doing the task yourself meanwhile.

whyNot.0: Surface decontamination needs IPC training to be done safely.
whyNot.1: Gloves don't replace training in the correct procedure.
whyNot.3: A calm explanation and suggested solution is better than refusing outright.

reteach.title: One Monday morning
reteach.question: How many duty 3 and duty 4 moments can you spot before the first coffee break?

blocks.body: At 8:45 the phone rings: someone wants to know if their neighbour is booked in. You politely don't confirm. At 9:00 an anxious patient arrives; you sit at her eye level, agree a stop signal and explain each step. At 9:40 you write up the notes as the dentist finishes. At 10:15 you notice the new trainee loading the washer-disinfector wrongly, so you show her how and check her next load. Four ordinary moments, all evidence.

blocks.text: Everyday moments count. You don't need a dramatic story to evidence duties 3 and 4; you need a real one you can explain clearly, with why you acted as you did.

explain.body: Read non-verbal cues, listen actively, and choose the right method for each patient. Use professional interpreters, not children or relatives, for clinical discussions.

test.q: Which is the best way to give an anxious patient a sense of control during treatment?
options: Agree a stop signal before you start
Keep explanations to a minimum
Ask them to keep their eyes closed throughout
Play loud music in the surgery
test.why: A stop signal, such as a raised hand, gives the patient control and reduces anxiety.

whyNot.1: Clear explanations usually reduce anxiety; leaving patients in the dark raises it.
whyNot.2: Closing their eyes doesn't give them control.
whyNot.3: Loud music makes communication harder and may not suit the patient.

explain.body: Share information only on a need-to-know basis, with consent or where the law requires. Keep records contemporaneous, complete, accurate and attributable, for 11 years. Correct errors openly.

test.q: How long are dental clinical records kept, following the NHS records guidance change in May 2023?
options: 2 years
5 years
11 years
15 years
test.why: Dental clinical records are kept for 11 years, changed from 15 years in May 2023.

whyNot.0: Two years applies to some finance records, not clinical records.
whyNot.1: Five years is too short for dental clinical records.
whyNot.3: Fifteen years was the old rule before May 2023.

explain.body: Management runs systems and tasks. Leadership influences people and sets direction. Anyone can show leadership, whatever their role.

test.q: Which statement about leadership in dental nursing is correct?
options: Only the practice manager can lead
Leadership and management mean the same
Leaders must have staff reporting to them
Any team member can show leadership
test.why: Leadership is about influence and responsibility, so any team member can show it, including a newly qualified nurse.

whyNot.0: Leadership isn't limited to the manager.
whyNot.1: Management runs systems; leadership influences people and direction.
whyNot.2: You can lead without line-managing anyone.

explain.body: When you supervise a colleague, you take responsibility for showing them how, checking their work and giving feedback. Delegate only to people who are trained, competent and indemnified.

test.q: Before delegating a task to a colleague, what must you be sure of?
options: That they are free at that moment
That they are trained and competent for it
That they have worked at the practice longest
That the dentist is out of the room
test.why: GDC guidance says you can only delegate to colleagues who are trained, competent and indemnified for the task.

whyNot.0: Being free doesn't make someone competent.
whyNot.2: Length of service doesn't guarantee training for that task.
whyNot.3: Whether the dentist is present is irrelevant to safe delegation.
